overview: Two State Department “List of Papers” index sheets summarize records concerning Japanese regulation of wireless communications during the 1930s. The indexed material covers Japanese radio laws, restrictions on radio equipment used by diplomatic missions, authorization of broadcast receiving sets at the Japanese Embassy in Washington and foreign missions in Japan, consultations with the Federal Radio Commission and the War and Navy Departments, and a 1938 amendment concerning medical-treatment telegrams and the Japanese hospitals authorized to transmit them.

subfiles.title: List of papers on Japanese radio laws and diplomatic receiving sets
subfiles.about: An index sheet lists correspondence about Japanese radio regulations and the installation of broadcast receiving equipment by diplomatic missions.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records a Japan despatch associated with Neville that enclosed earlier reporting and materials on Japanese radio laws. It also describes a Foreign Office circular regulating radio equipment at diplomatic missions in Japan and a request for information about comparable restrictions in the United States. Entries from October and November 1931 concern permission for broadcast receivers at the Japanese Embassy in Washington and circulation of the Japanese rules to the Federal Radio Commission and the War and Navy Departments.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet No. 4: medical-treatment wireless telegrams
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy in Japan (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: An index entry records a report on changes to Japanese wireless-telegram regulations governing medical-treatment messages.
subfiles.summary: The sheet indexes Japan message no. 0127, associated with Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and dated July 23, 1938. The message transmitted changes to wireless-telegram regulations concerning “medical treatment messages.” It also enclosed a list of hospitals in Japan designated to send and receive such telegrams.

interest: Although these are index sheets rather than the underlying correspondence, they provide a compact map of State Department handling of Japanese wireless regulation. They reveal both the diplomatic reciprocity involved in permitting embassy radio receivers and the interagency circulation of Japanese rules among civilian and military communications authorities. The 1938 reference to designated hospitals is especially useful evidence of the specialized regulation of international medical telegrams.
